matched_finding.description: Sample-size inconsistency in CREP procedure: The Method section creates a sample-size inconsistency: it states that all included studies collected the CREP-specified minimum of 120 participants, but the next subsection reports sample sizes ranging from 80 to 374, and Table 1 lists several replication Ns below 120 (specifically 90, 90, 80, 116, 94, 374, and 81). It is unclear whether 120 was a recruitment target, a raw-sample criterion, an analytic-N criterion, or an erroneous threshold. If these are the analytic or collected sample sizes relevant to inclusion, most of the included studies do not appear to have met the stated 120-participant minimum.
matched_finding.quote:
The CREP team specified the minimum sample size required for the replication; this size was generally set at the original study's sample size (which were small enough to be feasible for undergraduate student researchers, but set at 100 for larger studies). All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP ( 120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power), posted their raw dataset, and reported a summary of results.

## Participants in and Procedures of Forest and Wood (2012) CREP Replications

Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017 (see Table 1 for a list of the participating institutions). Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374 .

matched_finding.description: Post-hoc selection of heterogeneity estimator: The rationale for choosing REML over DL is framed in a data-dependent way. REML is a defensible estimator, but saying it was selected because it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for this dataset leaves unclear whether the estimator choice was made on methodological grounds or after comparing outputs. This matters because the estimator affects the random-effects weights, heterogeneity estimates, and interval estimates.
